name: Zero Trust and Network Segmentation
intent: Limit what one compromised machine can reach, by splitting the network into zones and, better, by letting each service accept only calls from the specific identities that need it, instead of trusting anything that is inside the network.
scenario: A shop runs 12 hosts: a web front end, a mobile gateway, five services, three data stores, a CI runner and a monitoring host. All of them sit on one internal network. An attacker takes over the search service through a flaw in a library it uses.
problem: On a flat internal network, being inside is treated as being trusted. The search service has no business talking to the orders database, yet nothing stops it, so one compromised host becomes a stepping stone to every other host. The question is not whether some host will be compromised, but how much of the system the attacker can reach from there: the blast radius.

howItWorks.title: The flat network: inside means trusted
howItWorks.text: Every host can open a connection to every other host, and services accept requests from any internal address. The perimeter (firewall, VPN) is the only control. Once an attacker is past it, or compromises any single host, they can scan and connect to everything, including the databases and the payment service.

howItWorks.title: Segmentation: zones with rules between them
howItWorks.text: Group hosts into zones (edge, app, data, operations) and allow only the zone-to-zone connections that are needed, for example edge to app and app to data, but not edge to data. It is simple to understand and cheap to enforce in a firewall or security group. Its limit is that inside a zone everything still trusts everything, and a zone rule is as broad as the zone.

howItWorks.title: Identity-based access: allow a named caller, not an address
howItWorks.text: Each service has a cryptographic identity, usually a short-lived certificate, and states exactly which callers may call it, and for what. With mutual TLS (mTLS) both sides present certificates, so the callee knows which service is calling rather than guessing from an IP address. The search service is then allowed to call the cache and nothing else, wherever it runs.

howItWorks.title: Zero trust: verify every request, assume breach
howItWorks.text: Zero trust is the idea behind it: network location grants nothing, and every request is authenticated and authorised on its own, with least privilege, and logged. It is not a product you buy. It is also not only about the network: a compromised service can still misuse the calls it is allowed to make, so each hop should check what the caller may ask for.

howItWorks.title: The extreme: a policy so strict that everything is an exception
howItWorks.text: If policy is detailed but nobody owns keeping it current, new legitimate calls break, and the fastest fix is a broad exception (allow this caller to reach the whole data zone). Enough exceptions and the policy is nearly as open as before, but harder to understand. Treat policy as code, change it with the service that needs it, review exceptions with an expiry, and measure how many paths nobody needs.

pros: A compromised host reaches only what its role needs, so incidents stay small
Identity survives moves between hosts, networks and clouds, where addresses do not
Every connection is authenticated and encrypted, which also helps against passive snooping inside the network
A clear, reviewable list of who may call whom doubles as documentation
cons: Certificates need issuing, short lifetimes and automated rotation, or they become an outage source
Policy has to be maintained as services change, and strictness without process breaks real traffic
Debugging a denied connection is harder than debugging a flat network
It does not stop a compromised service from abusing the calls it is allowed to make
whenToUse: Segmentation first, for any network with databases or admin tools that most hosts have no reason to reach
Identity-based access and mTLS for service-to-service traffic in larger or multi-team systems, or when the data is sensitive
whenNotToUse: Per-pair policy for a handful of services owned by one team, where zones plus authentication in the application are enough
A big-bang zero trust programme with no owner for policy and no way to see which flows are actually in use
pitfalls: Treating the VPN or the firewall as the whole security model
Segmenting into zones but leaving everything inside a zone open, and putting a CI runner or admin host that can reach everything in a zone of its own power
Granting an exception that is wider than the flow it unblocks, and never removing it
Enforcing by IP address in an environment where addresses are reused or spoofable, instead of by service identity
Long-lived certificates or shared service credentials that a stolen host can reuse for weeks
Forgetting that an allowed path can be pivoted through: one over-privileged service re-opens the whole graph

roles.label: Attacker
roles.description: Has taken over one host and looks for what else it can reach.

roles.label: Service
roles.description: An application that calls others and is called.

roles.label: Data store
roles.description: A database or cache holding sensitive data.

roles.label: Policy
roles.description: The firewall rules or service-identity allow-lists.

quiz.question: A team splits its network into edge, app and data zones and blocks edge to data. An attacker compromises one app service. Which statement is most accurate?
options: The attacker is contained to that one service, because zones isolate every host.
The attacker is blocked from every other app service, because the firewall separates them.
The attacker can still reach every other app service and the data zone, as those are allowed by zone rules.
The attacker cannot move at all, since a zone rule applies to the whole application.
quiz.explanation: Zone rules are as broad as the zone: inside the app zone hosts trust each other, and app to data is allowed. Segmentation shrinks the radius but does not contain a host to its own role. Per-service identity-based rules narrow it further.

quiz.question: What does mutual TLS between services give the callee that an IP allow-list does not?
options: A verified identity of the calling service, independent of its address
Protection against a service that is allowed to call you misusing that call
Automatic detection of a compromised host
A guarantee that no host in the same zone is compromised
quiz.explanation: Each side proves a certificate-backed identity, so policy can name the service rather than an address that may change or be reused. It says nothing about whether the caller is behaving, it does not detect compromise, and it makes no claim about other hosts.

quiz.question: A security team writes a very detailed per-flow policy, and new services keep breaking. Engineers start adding exceptions letting a caller reach a whole zone. What is the likely result and best response?
options: Safer overall, because every exception is logged, so leave it as it is
Equally safe, because exceptions only apply to the services that asked for them
A flat network, so remove the policy entirely and rely on the perimeter
A policy near as open as before and harder to read; own policy as code with the service and expire exceptions
quiz.explanation: Broad exceptions re-open paths nobody needs, so the strictness is mostly theatre. The fix is process: policy changes ship with the service that needs them, exceptions are narrow and expire, and unused paths are measured. Dropping the policy discards real protection.
